correctness.rationale: For each one-unit transfer, the two-species discovery-time survival numerator difference is exactly C(a-1,j-1)-C(b,j-1)≥0. Inverse-CDF coupling of the first two-type discovery times, followed by true conditional pair-type words and shared pair/other interleaving, proves the all-prefix path inequality with valid uniform-permutation marginals. Exact subset counting of one-to-two pair-species status shifts yields the nonnegative upper-tail kernel. Absence probabilities and Pascal give the exact expectation, including sharp strictness. Finite integer-majorization transfer decomposition and coupling gluing extend the result. The executed standalone verifier checked 150,643 exact tail equations on 1,846 distinct transfers, plus 280 exact two-type discovery-time equations. Finite checks are corroboration only.

originality.rationale: Literature-led comparison of the specific implication (a joint, simultaneous all-prefix coupling for uniform finite-census sampling without replacement, plus an exact nonnegative tail-improvement kernel) against full accessible arXiv:1608.00155, independent-trial majorization, and known multiple-hypergeometric observed-class formulas identified no statement covering this combination. Published research-record comparisons of occupancy and sampling diversity did not show covering implications. The 1986 hypergeometric paper and 1989 majorization sampling treatment were not materially inspectable as full texts, so a genuine residual equivalence risk remains; the assessment is not an independent exhaustive bibliographic certification.
residual_risks: Walton (1986) complete text not accessible; a theorem or appendix could subsume fixed-size tail dominance or joint coupling.
General majorization books and older finite-population sampling theses may contain equivalent coupling under alternate terminology; only extracts were accessible.
A positive proof and unsuccessful literature searches do not certify global originality. Independent specialist bibliographic review remains unperformed.

value.rationale: Finite-census richness accumulation is a central rarefaction statistic. The theorem upgrades the classical one-sample expected richness comparison to a coupling of every sample-size prefix and every discovery threshold simultaneously, with explicit nonnegative finite-sample tail effect for each integer balancing transfer. This describes how species-abundance evenness improves the whole distribution of richness accumulation, not merely its mean, and supplies a reproducible exact kernel. Variance or field-detection claims are excluded; no paper-sized downstream consequence is needed for this natural structural classification.
